findings.title: Options-object construction enables rejectOnClear by default
findings.cause: The options-object branch destructures `rejectOnClear = true` even though the documented and typed default is false.
findings.impact: Users calling `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` get pending promises rejected with AbortError when `clearQueue()` is called. That is a breaking behavior change from the documented default, and it can unexpectedly reject `Promise.all`/await chains.
findings.evidence: Current source sets the default at index.js:6-8 and rejects queued items at index.js:77-88. The public contract says `rejectOnClear` has default `false` in readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106. A focused probe printed `rejected:AbortError` for `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` after `clearQueue()`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: After installing dependencies, run: `node --input-type=module -e "import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const running = limit(() => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 25))); const pending = limit(() => 'ok'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); const race = await Promise.race([pending.then(() => 'fulfilled', error => 'rejected:' + error.name), new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve('pending'), 50))]); console.log(race); assert.equal(race, 'pending'); await running;"` It fails with actual `rejected:AbortError`.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation guard changed to `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`, so only truthy invalid values are rejected.
findings.impact: Plain JavaScript callers can pass `0`, `''`, or `null` for `rejectOnClear` and the limiter is constructed successfully, despite the runtime contract requiring a boolean. Those invalid values are silently treated as disabled behavior.
findings.evidence: index.js:12-14 only validates truthy values. index.d.ts:106 declares `rejectOnClear?: boolean`, and the previous runtime validation rejected every non-boolean. A focused assertion expecting TypeError for `0`, `''`, and `null` failed immediately with `Missing expected exception (TypeError)` for `0`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `node --input-type=module -e "import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, '', null]) { assert.throws(() => pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}), TypeError); }"`

findings.title: limit.map omits mapper indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The map implementation now passes `index` only when `Array.isArray(iterable)` is true, substituting `undefined` for Sets, array iterators, and other iterables.
findings.impact: The public API says `limit.map(iterable, mapperFunction)` passes each item and its index for any iterable. Mappers over Sets, generator results, or iterator objects now receive `undefined` indexes, which breaks ordering, labeling, batching, and key-generation use cases.
findings.evidence: index.js:106-113 computes `iterableIsArray` and passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`. readme.md:78-85 and index.d.ts:40-43 state that the mapper receives the item value and index for an iterable. A focused probe produced `["a:undefined","b:undefined","c:undefined"]` for `new Set(['a','b','c'])`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `node --input-type=module -e "import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import pLimit from './index.js'; const mapped = await pLimit(2).map(new Set(['a','b','c']), (value, index) => value + ':' + index); console.log(JSON.stringify(mapped)); assert.deepEqual(mapped, ['a:0','b:1','c:2']);"`

findings.title: limitFunction drops all caller arguments
findings.cause: `limitFunction` returns a zero-argument wrapper and invokes `function_()` instead of forwarding `...arguments_`.
findings.impact: Any reusable limited function that needs input parameters receives none. This breaks the typed signature and documented recipe pattern such as `limitedFetchUrl(url)`.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-125 returns `() => limit(() => function_())`. index.d.ts:133-136 declares the returned function as `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`, and recipes.md:161-163 demonstrates calling the limited function with `url`. A focused probe returned `[]` from an async rest-argument function called as `limited('alpha', 'beta')`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `node --input-type=module -e "import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async (...args) => args, {concurrency: 1}); const result = await limited('alpha', 'beta'); console.log(JSON.stringify(result)); assert.deepEqual(result, ['alpha','beta']);"`

findings.title: Infinity is no longer accepted as an unlimited concurrency value
findings.cause: The concurrency validator now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)` and removed the explicit `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance.
findings.impact: Callers using `pLimit(Infinity)` to intentionally disable limiting while keeping the same API path now get a TypeError at construction time. This is an edge-case behavioral regression from the repository baseline.
findings.evidence: Current index.js:127-130 rejects anything that is not a positive integer. `git show HEAD:index.js` shows the previous validator allowed `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`. A focused assertion `assert.doesNotThrow(() => pLimit(Infinity))` failed with `TypeError: Expected \`concurrency\` to be a number from 1 and up`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `node --input-type=module -e "import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import pLimit from './index.js'; assert.doesNotThrow(() => pLimit(Infinity));"`
